title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Session with CFA Society, United Kingdom on June 12, 2024
summary: Pabrai recounts how his magician grandfather and serially-bankrupt entrepreneur father shaped him, his move from Tellabs to TransTech to Pabrai Investment Funds, and his style shifts from tech growth (1994-99) to deep value (37% a year 1999-2007) and back toward quality. He explains his current ~$1 billion portfolio (600 million in three Turkish names, 300 million in coal), the IPSCO-to-CONSOL story, why macro is noise, and how he built his checklist from the mistakes of great investors.

ideas.idea: Being 'elected' to his father's nightly board of directors at 12-13, trying to keep a dying business alive one more day, gave him the ability to crack business models fast in unfamiliar industries.
ideas.detail: His father started, grew and bankrupted at least a dozen companies in a dozen industries, was brilliant at spotting offering gaps (e.g. a Dubai gold jewelry factory exploiting a 2% duty arbitrage that vanished once competitors arrived) and took him on jewelry sales calls at 16. 'I finished several MBAs by the time I was 18.'

ideas.idea: In a large business only the people who create and the people who sell matter; never be in the fill-in-the-blanks middle, and eventually capture the spoils yourself.
ideas.detail: His father's advice at 24 pushed him from R&D to international sales at Tellabs and then to start TransTech as low-risk as possible, finding an offering gap; Pabrai Investment Funds itself filled an offering gap.

ideas.idea: The big aha about Buffett was that he uses the same brain cells as a business strategist but never has to execute; investing is strategy with leverage and no heavy lifting.
ideas.detail: He heard of Buffett and Munger 'exactly about 30 years ago'; he sold a small piece of TransTech for $1 million in 1994 and it became about $13 million by 2000, leading to the funds.

ideas.idea: An investor's job is to look for anomalies, things that make no sense; whatever criterion you set, Mr. Market will serve up companies that fit it.
ideas.detail: Coke traded at 40-50x in 1999-2000 and about 7x in the 1970s-early 80s; any random stock's 52-week range is like 75 to 150 though the business cannot change that much in a year, because auction-driven markets deviate from fundamentals. Whether you want trailing PE of 1, 0.1 or one-third of book, among 50,000 global equities you will find them.

ideas.idea: He was 80-90% in tech growth stocks from 1994-99, switched entirely to deep value at the top of the bubble, then stayed in deep value about six years too long.
ideas.detail: A failed private dot-com (he lost ~$3 million, outside investors ~$2 million) gave him a three-month look-ahead at the bubble. On March 9, 2000, the day NASDAQ peaked, Berkshire hit a multi-year low as people sold it for pets.com. Buying funeral homes and oil tankers, the funds did 37% a year before fees from 1999-2007 with no down years; by 2011-12 he should have gone back to better businesses.

ideas.idea: Value and growth are joined at the hip; every business is worth its discounted future cash flows, and the bias should be toward great growing businesses with high returns on equity even at a higher multiple.
ideas.detail: The controversy is only what the cash flows are and how certain you are; even Nvidia's insiders cannot say what revenue looks like in 5-10 years. Paying more for growth can beat a very low PE on something flat or declining, but remain agnostic and look at the landscape.

ideas.idea: Investing is opportunistic with no strategic plan; markets today are heavily picked over, so finding one good idea a year is doing well.
ideas.detail: Munger said he and Buffett 'would do terribly' starting today versus the 1970s when 1974-75 was 'orgasmic' for value investors; there are now more mutual funds, hedge funds and analysts (3-4 to 1) than stocks. If he finds nothing he hopes to be smart enough to sit in treasuries.

ideas.idea: His ~$1 billion portfolio is 'the weirdest you can think of': about 600 million in three Turkish names and 300 million in three or four coal names, with coal built from zero in 13 months.
ideas.detail: A May 2023 tweet comparing David Einhorn's CONSOL Energy position to his old IPSCO bet started the coal work; he spent eight months and many mine visits in Appalachia getting his arms around coal and now has 30% there.

ideas.idea: IPSCO (2003-04) was the ideal bet: $15 a share in cash plus contractually firm $15 a year of cash flow for two years against a $40 stock, so plant and inventory came free.
ideas.detail: Pipeline purchase orders gave extreme clarity, unlike Apple or Microsoft guidance; his whole analysis was wanting to see how Mr. Market priced it with $45 on the balance sheet in two years. It hit $60 after another $15 guidance, then a Swedish company bid $160 and he sold 'in one femtosecond'; per Mark Twain, fiction makes sense but reality never does.

ideas.idea: CONSOL Energy is 'IPSCO is back' with a big extra positive: contracted forward sales a year or more out combined with furious share buybacks.
ideas.detail: Most of the next 12 months of sales are already contracted, with some visibility two to three years out, and all the cash goes to buybacks. Very few management teams are enlightened enough to buy back; one CEO complained the cash 'just goes into the ether'.

ideas.idea: Start with what is hated and unloved; a beaten-down market is mostly correctly beaten down, but you only need one or two babies thrown out with the bathwater.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: His first Istanbul trip in 2018 came from Turkey screening super cheap despite inflation and currency collapse; he asked a Ben Graham disciple friend to show only companies he actually owned, in order. High-quality businesses like Coke bottlers and dominant beer brands with mostly non-Turkish revenue were punished merely for being listed in Istanbul.

ideas.idea: Macro, CPI and interest rates are at the noise level; the less clutter in your mind, the better, so focus energy on the micro of one business.
ideas.detail: It is hard enough to figure out what one simple business will do long term; overlaying macro mostly leads you astray. Understand the business, know what it is worth, then try to buy it at a half or a third of that.

ideas.idea: Learn from mistakes but not too much, since a 40-50% error rate is par for the course; the richer data set is the mistakes of the greats, converted into checklist questions.
ideas.detail: For each Berkshire mistake he asked what was obvious at the time yet missed: Dexter Shoe became 'can this business be decimated by low-cost foreign manufacturers?' and US Air became 'is it unionized, is it a low-cost operator?' This mirrors how the FAA built aviation checklists after crashes.

ideas.idea: He prefers the FAA's pragmatic approach of pricing a human life (about $1.8 million a decade ago) to the nuclear industry's 'infinite' value, which meant nuclear never got a fair shake.
ideas.detail: The FAA mandates fixes only when their cost is below expected lives saved times that value; treating a life as worth infinity is why a very clean energy solution stalled.

ideas.idea: Going from entrepreneur to investor is easier than the reverse; Buffett is a better businessman because he is an investor and vice versa.
ideas.detail: Running lemonade stands at 12 is very useful. Buffett said that if you deliver above-market returns, investors will swim to you through shark-infested waters even if you are a leper.

ideas.idea: To grow a fund under solicitation rules, deliver returns, directly 'ask for the order' from existing investors, and have them tell friends and family to call you.
ideas.detail: After a ~70% first year he asked investors for more money and for introductions; with 15-20% returns plus 10-15% inflows, assets double every two years. He went from 8 investors to 17 to about 25 in two years, and adds 'focus on friends, family and food, especially the food'. Bill Gates: even a monopoly has to ask for the order.

ideas.idea: Turkey is not a monolith: two of his three Turkish bets earn most income outside Turkey, so the portfolio is effectively five bets, and he cannot construct a scenario in which even one fails.
ideas.detail: Most of his net worth is in the funds, so he has multiple incentives not to be wrong. The coal companies have no debt and net cash, unusual for miners, and businesses with no debt are anti-fragile.

ideas.idea: He expected the lira to keep collapsing (3 to the dollar in 2018, now approaching 33) and concluded 180-190 of ~200 listed Turkish companies were uninvestable, so he bought only businesses unaffected by or benefiting from devaluation.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Persistence through negative headlines came from being heavily up in dollar terms; the handful of companies with euro revenues or hard assets get tailwinds rather than headwinds.

ideas.idea: TAV Airports has euro revenues and lira costs, so its costs decline in the inflationary environment, and its outright purchase of Almaty airport during COVID was a rare bargain.
ideas.detail: Most private airports are build-operate-transfer concessions, but Almaty was bought outright for $400 million at zero passenger traffic, plus ~$200 million of CapEx for a new terminal; on a bad day it would fetch $3-6 billion. Two Harvard Business School cases cover TAV.

ideas.idea: A Coke bottler is resilient to any currency or even a global thermonuclear event: survivors would still trade labor for a Coke, and Coca-Cola would still own the trademark.
ideas.detail: The Turkish bottler is number one with all bottling rights in Pakistan, half of Bangladesh and eight or nine other countries; Coke has been around 140 years and is not going anywhere for another 140. Iconic assets at valuations that make no sense are why he invested.

ideas.idea: His Turkish warehouse stake cost $8 million for one-third of 12 million square feet of prime real estate now approaching $2 billion in liquidation value.
ideas.detail: Tenants are Amazon, Ikea, Carrefour, Toyota and Mercedes on long, inflation-indexed leases; 'I could not find a way that it was going to go away suddenly.'
